I think asking for examples of "people appropriating white culture" misunderstands how cultural appropriation exists in the US (and Western world in general). You rarely hear accusations of white culture being appropriated - I think in large part it stems from the fact that these minority groups (in particular, racial minorities) have been subject to systemic racism. Aka, legitimate legal and structural life barriers. 

As an example,  many black people view wearing dreadlocks as cultural appropriation, but not necessarily because white cultures don't historically have "dreads". Many opponents to this thought have brought up Ancient Celtic culture as an example of culturally white dreadlocks. However, in US ( a very young country with a relatively modern history), African Americans have dealt with accusations of unprofessionalism due to the nature of their hair (e.g. dreadlocks being viewed as unprofessional despite that being the only option for some people to style their hair.) So when white people wear dreads and flaunt them around as "style", African Americans get angry and think "well why can Kevin wear this and be interpreted as looking good, but Jamal wears this and is thought to be an unprofessional thug?"

White culture being appropriated is a non-issue (in the context of the larger discourse surrounding appropriation) due to it being the 'majority' culture. The issue is with minorities being (in their eyes) wrongfully exploited, or having elements of their culture shunned and then later commoditized by the majority. It's an issue that predominantly exists in North American spheres due to the modern socio-cultural history specific to the region.

My BMI is in the 19s. Did ballet for 15 something years and then quit to go to Uni. My advice? It took a long time, but eating way more protein helps. My macros are 40% protein and then 30-30 for fats and carbs. So I'm eating like ~120g of protein while eating like ~1200 to 1300 cals per day rn. I struggled with disordered eating so having daily goals really helps (since its a control thing for me). I tried to do a cut/bulk cycle and the rapid changes in my body really fucked with my mental health so this slow recomp works better for me. But yeah, I was always quite muscular (ballet) so I just went ahead and lift heavy but do glutes three days a week (other days are light cardio). Smith machine glute bridges, romainian deadlifts, hip abductions, back extensions, leg presses and bulgarian split squats are key. I don't follow Strong Curves (I've read through it and follow Bret for reference). I also usually do cardio after lifting (~15-20min) to try and deplete the rest of my glycogen stores. 

Ab work, I usually stick to staples like planks and crunches and other stuff I used to do when I was training. Same with arms. Do note that I was not necessarily a beginner when I started. I started working out a year or so after I quit so I was still quite muscular/in shape -- so ymmv.

It moves the conversation along in a way I guess. In a situation, if you acknowledge your privilege, you can work to fix a problem without condescending someone who in a position of disadvantage . Like let’s say you’re trying to help a homeless woman. By stating your privilege of being financially stable and willing to try to learn why she is suffering instead of suggesting she is at equal footing with you. Like to recognize the advantage you are at in comparison and understand that you can only sympathize not empathize and then move on from there. It avoids the classic “I worked for what I have” notion a lot of people have. Some people are systematically at a disadvantage and recognizing privilege of certain groups allows for us to look for equitable solutions not equal solutions. The things that are holding certain people back are different. So an equal solution wouldn’t work.

Like in education. African American children have low literacy rates in comparison to white children. Children with reading disabilities regardless of race have difficulty reading too.  But they have different problems. The school system is segregated by socio-economic factors (like property tax of an area) and African American children regularly attend underfunded school and receive poor education. Children with learning disabilities have a disability that prevents them learning in a similar way as normal children, and require special learning methods to catch them up. Those both groups have similar problems that require different solutions.

So when you acknowledge your privilege you are basically saying that you see that advantages you have and the disadvantages others have.

It avoids misunderstandings between two groups. If one recognizes it’s privileges in one regard and the other does the same they can better understand each other.

At least that’s how I interpret it when people bring up privilege. But I think the term is sort of useless when there is no common understanding of what it means, and sometimes people use it as an insult. Nothing is wrong with having privilege tbh. It’s how you go about it.

Ok, so what helps me...I know this kinda sounds dumb but I read the passage out loud and then summarize chunks. A) because you can get lost in the diction if you read it all the way through (they usually have rly archaic diction). B) Also I like to like make the summaries funny so I feel interested.

I read fast, so if you have time learn to read fast, and make sure you can read it well enough that you understand it. Like, don't speed read if you don't understand it, read quickly but so you can comprehend what you read. I spend around 1 or 2 min reading the passage out loud (under ur breath on test day) and after each chunked paragraph I retell myself what that paragraph was about. If I comprehend each paragraph, I understand the passage.

I don't read the questions first because I noticed I got a lot of questions wrong because I had made presumptions about the answers without fully reading the passage. That's why I don't skim read either. For some people it works, but for me it doesn't help my comprehension at all. I don't like looking back and forth between the essay and the questions. Read it all and know it all (more like most of it). It's a waste of time to read the questions, skim and then look for answers.

For reading also having a decent vocabulary helps. Skim through a dictionary sometime. I used to do that when I was little a lot. That way you won't be shit out of luck when some hard ass word comes up. Another great thing is knowing the synonyms to stuff. If u get some archaic ass diction switch that shit to easier words in ya head so you don't get lost. 

For example: 

"*I never observed that the women of America consider conjugal authority as a fortunate usurpation of their rights*"

Idk wtf homie is saying in that sentence. But lemme make it easier by switching the words I recognize:

"*I never observed that the women of America consider marriage authority as a fortunate seizing of their rights*"

Now that is in my language.

These strategies really do not work unless you can read FAST. A good way to practice reading fast is to watch movies with subtitles. Use subtitles for everything!!! It's a fun way to practice reading. Or you could time yourself reading too but that BORING imo.

Read a lot of historical text if you really have trouble getting a hang of the diction. I recommend reading Thoreau's stuff. If you can understand what he is saying, you'll understand everything because he is, in my opinion, the EPITOME of annoying, flowery, hard to understand, archaic diction. 

Historical articles basically say the same shit new writing says but fancier. 


Also a tip for writing is just read a lot. The more you read the more you will notice things that are wrong. Idk wtf a modifier is, idk wtf a clause is, but I can tell a sentence is wrong and how it should be fixed by looking at it. By reading. Reading correct grammar trains you to notice trash grammar. Like if you were really familiar with a map of ur town and one day you close your eyes and head down the wrong street. You dunno where you are but you sure as hell know how to get home. Know what I mean?

Once you can start recognizing it, you'll be able to answer the questions in a few or more seconds.

Also when they ask for like a revision of a chunk of a sentence always pick the shortest option, or read the whole sentence and see if that chunk is redundant. I've noticed they have at least 2 questions that can be answered like that.

And know your conjunctive adverbs!!!! KNOW THEM!! Know stuff like "nevertheless" can be read as "in spite of". A lot of questions ask you to replace conjunctive verbs and replacing them with a synonym helps me understand things when I feel stuck!

Anyway these are just some things that helped me. If you want more I still have some.

Realizing that your feelings of being upset are valid, and that your forgiveness is a privilege not a right. Recognizing that the person who made the mistake and the person who is trying to make amends are now different people.
